name: Modern Defense
summary: 1...g6 and 2...Bg7. You hand White the centre on purpose, then spend the game proving it is a target rather than an asset.
coach_note: Klausies — listen. In the Modern you are not being passive, you are being patient. White builds a big centre because you let him, and every pawn he pushes is one more thing he has to defend. Your bishop on g7 is already pointing at it before the game starts. Get ...a6 and ...b5 in, put the bishop on b7, and then hit the middle with ...c5 or ...e5. The centre falls, the long diagonal opens, and everything you have been doing quietly starts working at once.
scheme: The g7-bishop is the opening. Every plan is about the a1-h8 diagonal and what stands on it.
The standard build: ...g6, ...Bg7, ...d6, ...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7, ...Nd7 — then a break.
Two levers, and you need one of them: ...c5 against d4, or ...e5 when White cannot support the centre.
The recurring trick: ...c5 and if dxc5 then ...Qa5, taking the pawn back with tempo against c3.
Do not castle into an attack you can see coming. In the long-castling lines Black often leaves the king in the middle or goes queenside instead.
reading: White's fourth move usually announces the whole plan — Be3 means a storm, f4 means a rollover, Nf3 with Be2 means a long game.
Count the defenders of d4 before every break. ...c5 works when d4 is short of them.
If White castles long, it is a race and tempi decide it; if White castles short, it is a manoeuvring game and you have time.

looks.name: The 150 Attack
looks.tell: Be3 on move 4, then Qd2. The moment those two appear together, the rest is written: f3, Bh6, O-O-O, h4-h5.
looks.white_idea: Trade off your g7-bishop with Bh6, castle queenside, and roll the h-pawn at your king. It needs no theory from White, which is exactly why you will meet it more than anything else.
plans: Get ...a6 and ...b5 in before anything else. The attack on your king only wins if it arrives first, so start yours on move four.
Answer h4 with ...h5. It costs a tempo and buys the whole kingside: without h4-h5 the storm has no battering ram.
Bishop to b7, knight to d7, and keep the king in the centre or send it queenside. Castling kingside here is walking into the attack.
Break with ...c5 when d4 is short of defenders, and the long diagonal opens onto a king that has nowhere to hide.
strategic: This is a race between two attacks on opposite wings, and races are counted in tempi, not evaluated in pawns. A move that improves a piece but does not advance the attack is a move you have lost.
The c3-knight is the shield in front of White's king. Everything you own should end up pointing at it: the b-pawn, the queen from a5, a rook on the b- or c-file, and the bishop once the centre opens.
When White plays Bh6, taking is usually right. Your bishop is worth more than his, but a queen on h6 is a queen that has left the queenside — and the queenside is where you are playing.

tactics.name: ...h5 kills the storm
tactics.point: The entire attack is h4-h5 opening the h-file. One pawn move stops it, and White has to find a different idea — usually a slow one, which suits you.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 f3 Nd7 h4 h5

tactics.name: ...b4 hits the shield
tactics.point: The knight on c3 is the only thing between your pieces and his king. Hitting it with a pawn means it moves on your terms, not his.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 f3 Nd7 h4 h5 O-O-O Bb7 Bh6 b4

looks.watch: Do not castle kingside here out of habit. In this line the safest king is often the one still on e8, and the second safest is on the queenside behind your own pawns.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 b5 f3 Nd7 h4 h5 O-O-O Bb7

looks.name: The Austrian Attack
looks.tell: f4 on move four. Three pawns abreast on e4, d4 and f4.
looks.white_idea: Take every square in the centre, then push e5 or f5 and squash you before you develop. It looks terrifying and it is genuinely dangerous if you let it roll.
plans: Hit it immediately with ...c5. Do not develop first — a centre like this has to be challenged before it advances.
After dxc5, ...Qa5 takes the pawn back with tempo because the knight on c3 is pinned to the king.
Then complete development with ...Nc6 and ...Nf6 and aim everything at e4, which is the pawn holding the rest up.
If White pushes e5 anyway, take — ...dxe5 — and let the g7-bishop and the d-file do the work.
strategic: An over-extended centre is not space, it is a list of things to defend. Each of e4, d4 and f4 needs pieces behind it, and pieces tied to pawns are not attacking anything.
The f4-pawn takes the e3 square away from White's own bishop and leaves the a7-g1 diagonal and the e3 square soft. Your queen on c5 sits on that diagonal for a reason.
Trade when it helps: every trade makes a big centre less of an attacking force and more of a long-term weakness.

tactics.name: The pin that wins the pawn back
tactics.point: The knight on c3 is pinned against the king on e1, so it cannot defend anything. That is what makes ...Qxc5 free — and it is the same trick that appears against 3.h4.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 f4 c5 dxc5 Qa5

tactics.name: Why you take on e5
tactics.point: If White answers ...c5 by pushing past with d5, the centre is closed and ...e5 seizes the squares it left behind. Locked centre, wing play — and your wing is the kingside with ...f5.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 f4 c5 d5 e5

looks.watch: The one thing that loses here is developing quietly and letting White play e5 for free. If you have not hit the centre by move six, you are already worse.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 f4 c5 dxc5 Qa5 Bd3 Qxc5 Qe2 Nc6 Nf3 Nf6

looks.name: Classical — Nf3 and a quiet bishop
looks.tell: Nf3 early with Be2 or Bd3, and White castles short.
looks.white_idea: No attack, just more space and a solid centre. White intends to be slightly better for fifty moves and win a technical game.
plans: Because White castled short there is no race, so take your time: ...a6, ...b5, ...Bb7, ...Nd7, and only then a break.
Play ...e6 to give the position a second break. With both ...c5 and ...e5 available White cannot cover everything.
Aim the b7-bishop and a rook on the c-file at c3 and e4, and wait for a moment when d4 is short of defenders.
This is the line where the Hippo set-up — pawns on a6, b5, d6, e6, g6 with both bishops fianchettoed — is fully playable.
strategic: With no attack coming, the winner is whoever breaks at the better moment. Improve every piece first; the break keeps.
White's extra centre pawn is only an asset while it is mobile. Fix it, blockade it, and it turns into a target.
Do not trade the g7-bishop for a knight without a reason. In a slow position it is the piece that will decide the game.

tactics.name: ...b4 asks the question
tactics.point: When White plays a4 to stop the pawn, push past it. The c3-pawn has to decide, and whichever way it goes, the long diagonal gets a little clearer.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Be2 a6 O-O b5 Bd3 Bb7 c3 Nd7 Re1 e6 a4 b4

looks.watch: The danger in quiet lines is drifting. If you find yourself shuffling with no break in sight, you have already lost the thread — pick ...c5 or ...e5 and prepare it properly.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Be2 a6 O-O b5 Bd3 Bb7 c3 Nd7 Re1 e6

looks.name: Bc4 — pressure on f7
looks.tell: The bishop goes to c4 rather than e2 or d3, staring at f7.
looks.white_idea: Hit the weakest square in your camp before you finish developing, usually with Qf3 or Qe2 and an e5 push behind it.
plans: Play ...e6 first. It takes d5 and f5 away from White and, more to the point, it un-weakens f7.
Develop the knight to e7 rather than f6 — it keeps the long diagonal clear and covers d5 and f5.
Then ...b6 and ...Bb7, and the second bishop joins the same diagonal battle.
Once f7 is safe the c4-bishop is just a bishop, and it is often the piece with the fewest squares.
strategic: Every move White spends on the f7 square is a move not spent on the centre. Defuse it and you are simply a tempo up on a normal Modern.
A knight on e7 looks modest and is not: it supports ...d5 and ...f5, and it never blocks the bishop.
The c4-bishop has to watch out for ...d5 and ...b5 coming with tempo. Those moves are worth more here than elsewhere.

tactics.name: ...e6 before anything else
tactics.point: Not the natural ...Nf6. With the bishop on c4 and a queen coming to f3 or e2, f7 is the point of the whole set-up, and ...e6 answers it once and for all.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Bc4 e6

looks.watch: Tricks on f7 only work while your king is in the middle and the f7-pawn has one defender. Solve that first and the line loses its teeth.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Bc4 e6 Nf3 Ne7 O-O O-O Bg5 h6 Be3 b6

looks.name: The big centre with c4
looks.tell: c4 comes out early, usually move three, before the knights.
looks.white_idea: Build the whole thing — c4, d4, e4 — and play a King's Indian with an extra tempo, hoping you do not know King's Indian plans.
plans: Answer with ...d6 and ...e5. If White locks with d5 you have a King's Indian, and King's Indian plans are the clearest in chess.
Once the centre is shut, race: knights regroup towards the kingside, then ...f5, ...f4 and ...g5-g4.
The knight to c5 hits e4 and eyes d3 and a4 — it is the best piece in the structure.
Keep the queenside closed if you can. Every file White opens there is a file he attacks down.
strategic: A locked centre means neither side can be punished in the middle, so slow moves on your own wing cost nothing. That is the licence to attack with pawns in front of your own king.
It is a pure race and the evaluation barely matters — what matters is who arrives first, and the counting is concrete.
Your bishop on g7 is temporarily a bad piece behind the e5 pawn. It comes alive the moment the f-file opens, which is another reason ...f5 is the move.

tactics.name: The knight lands on c5
tactics.point: It hits e4 and cannot be driven off by a pawn without White making b4 a permanent hole. That is what an outpost is worth.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 c4 d6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nd7 Be2 Ne7 O-O O-O d5 Nc5

looks.watch: Do not open the queenside for him. ...c6 and ...cxd5 hands White the c-file, which is the road to your king.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 c4 d6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 Nd7 Be2 Ne7 O-O O-O d5 Nc5

looks.name: The early h4
looks.tell: h4 on move three, before a single piece comes out.
looks.white_idea: Push h4-h5, rip open the h-file and mate you before the opening finishes. Entirely a bluff if you know the answer, and entirely winning if you do not.
plans: Meet a wing attack with a counter in the centre. ...c5 is the move, and it is a principle rather than a memorised line.
After dxc5 the check on a5 picks the pawn straight back, because nothing on c3 can interpose yet.
Develop fast while White's h-pawn sits where it cannot help: ...Nc6, ...d6, and the queen retreats to a5 where it is safe and useful.
You can also answer ...h5 to stop it outright, but the central counter is stronger — punish the loss of time.
strategic: A flank attack launched before development is refuted in the centre. That is not a Modern Defense rule, it is the rule, and this position is the cleanest example of it you will get.
White's h4 does nothing for his king, his development or his centre. Every move you spend developing while he spends moves on the h-file is a move you are ahead.
Once you are two tempi up in an open position, trade into anything — the attack evaporates and the extra development remains.

tactics.name: ...c5 and the check that collects
tactics.point: With no knight on c3 yet, the check comes with the pawn hanging behind it. White has to block and you take on c5 with a free tempo.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 h4 c5 dxc5 Qa5+

looks.watch: If you answer h4 by castling kingside you are helping him. Leave the king where it is until the h-file question is settled.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 h4 c5 dxc5 Qa5+ Nc3 Qxc5 Nf3 Nc6 Be3 Qa5 Qd2 d6

looks.name: The Monkey's Bum
looks.frequency: rare, but it mates you if you miss it
looks.tell: 2.Bc4 and 3.Qf3 — bishop and queen both aimed at f7 before anything else moves.
looks.white_idea: Qxf7 mate, right now. It is a one-move threat with a silly name, and it is genuinely mate if you develop normally. The answer is not to defend f7 with a piece but to cut the bishop off from it.
plans: See the threat first: Qxf7 is mate, supported by the bishop on c4, with no square for the king.
...e6 answers it, and not by giving the king air: the pawn stands on the c4-bishop's diagonal, so f7 loses its supporter. Qxf7+ is then met by Kxf7, winning the queen.
Then ...Ne7 and ...d5 hit the bishop and the centre at once, and White's queen on f3 turns out to be badly placed.
Trade the light-squared bishops and White has nothing left but a lost tempo and a queen that has to move again.
strategic: An attack with two pieces against a castled-nowhere king is not an attack, it is an inconvenience. Answer it accurately once and White is simply worse.
Every White piece here is aimed at one square, and the two need each other. Take the bishop out of the equation and the queen alone attacks a square the king already defends.
Gaining time on the queen is the theme: ...d5 and ...Nf5 or ...Nc6 all come with tempo because she has no good home.

tactics.name: 3...e5?? is mate on the spot
tactics.point: The most natural developing move in the position loses the game immediately. This is the one line in the Modern where you must know the move rather than work it out.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 Bc4 Bg7 Qf3 e5 Qxf7#

tactics.name: 3...e6 is the move
tactics.point: The pawn on e6 cuts the c4-bishop off from f7, so the square is defended by the king alone. The capture that was mate a move ago now simply hangs the queen — and Kxf7 is Black's only legal move, which tells you how forced it is.
tactics.line_san: e4 g6 Bc4 Bg7 Qf3 e6 Qxf7+ Kxf7

looks.watch: This is the only line here worth memorising outright. Everything else in the Modern you can reason your way through; this one you either know or lose.
looks.line_san: e4 g6 Bc4 Bg7 Qf3 e6 d4 Ne7 Ne2 d5 exd5 exd5 Bb5+ Bd7 Bxd7+ Nxd7
